name: Ashurbanipal
role: Neo-Assyrian king, ruling from 669/668 BCE into the 630s BCE
summary: Ashurbanipal presented royal authority as divinely appointed and celebrated conquest, tribute and temple patronage. His inscriptions justify violent punishment of rebels, while his correspondence also emphasizes royal favors and protection for loyal communities.

more-religion-public.rationale: Prism B, i 14–26 boasts of temple restoration and increased offerings.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: His royal library preserves Mesopotamian scholarly and religious texts; this does not by itself establish a position about preserving national traditions generally.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Prism B, i 1–13 celebrates his kingship and descent from royal ancestors.

democracy-best.rationale: Inferred: his claim that the gods established his royal rule conflicts with making popular choice the highest governing authority.

right-to-secede.rationale: Inferred: his enforcement of Assyrian overlordship against Babylon’s revolt denies its claimed freedom to depart.

political-violence-never.rationale: His annals praise military destruction of rebels and deliberate terror against resisting cities.

separate-church-state.rationale: Prism B, i 14–26 joins royal government to his priestly service and temple patronage.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Prism E records incorporating conquered territory into Assyria; Prism B celebrates foreign subjugation.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: His correspondence treats royal favors and subjects’ reciprocal obligations as binding personal relationships, reinforced through loyalty treaties.

bound-labor.rationale: Captive enslavement and corvée evidence do not directly answer whether agricultural tenants should be legally bound to a lord’s land.

national-self-determination.rationale: Inferred: his demand that foreign rulers accept his imperial yoke conflicts with a universal right to independent national rule.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Prism B, v 25–77 presents prayer and Ishtar’s prophetic answer as guides to military policy.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Inferred: he grounds authority in divine appointment and imposed submission, rather than requiring the consent of subjects.

population-transfer.rationale: Prism B, iii 14–15 records removing the people of Qirbit and settling them in Egypt.

death-penalty.rationale: The annals describe killing captives and rebels, but do not establish a position on execution following conviction for the gravest crimes.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Prism B, iv 18–26 praises sending grain to famine-stricken Elam and sheltering its refugees.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Ito’s account of the Babylonian revolt documents his military suppression of his brother’s attempt to escape Assyrian overlordship.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Ito, pp. 100–101 and 231, analyzes his letters’ representation of himself as created and nurtured by goddesses.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Prism B, iii 1–2 imposes additional horses as tribute after a foreign ruler submits.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Prism B, i 91–95 celebrates killing and flaying inhabitants of rebellious Egyptian cities.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Prism B, vi 83–87 explicitly links mutilation and flaying to insults against his gods.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Prism B, i 6–13 explicitly credits the gods with establishing and magnifying his kingship.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The surviving succession record shows his accession under his father’s dynastic settlement and continuation through royal sons.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Evidence that women owned property in contemporary Assyria does not establish this king’s position on equal inheritance rights.

notes: The royal inscriptions are commissioned self-presentations and often contain propagandistic claims; high confidence identifies what he claimed or endorsed, rather than independently verifying every event. Later scholarly descriptions are medium at most. Four explicit historical deductions are low and do not count toward salience. Neither the apolitical early-exit rule nor assumptions about generic Assyrian society are used. All statements were reviewed; modern institutions and issue-specific positions without matching personal evidence remain null. Regnal chronology is disputed; the catalog birth date is approximate.
